cases.note: cloud metadata

cases.note: IPv6 ULA

cases.note: DNS rebinding; resolve-then-pin is the defence

cases.input: https://public.example.com/repo.git redirecting to http://10.0.0.1/
cases.note: redirects must be disabled, not followed-then-checked

cases.input: ext::sh -c id
cases.note: 🛑 exit criterion 1 of 5. git's <transport>::<address> syntax runs git-remote-ext, which runs the rest as a shell command. Must be refused on the RAW string: parse_url reports no scheme for it, so a check that waited for a parsed scheme would never fire

cases.input: file:///etc/passwd
cases.note: 🛑 exit criterion 2 of 5. Local file disclosure. Distinct from git_url-009 because execution and disclosure are different capabilities and an operator triaging an alert needs to know which fired

cases.input: https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/repo.git
cases.note: 🛑 exit criterion 3 of 5. Cloud instance metadata, which on most providers returns role credentials to an unauthenticated GET. Its own identifier rather than link_local, because 169.254.169.254 is a credential-theft primitive and 169.254.0.0/16 is a misconfiguration

cases.input: a TTL-0 DNS name answering 93.184.216.34 then 127.0.0.1
cases.note: 🛑 exit criterion 4 of 5. Distinct from the address identifiers: those fire on the FIRST answer, this one on a second answer that disagrees with it. Resolve-then-pin already makes the second answer unusable; this turns a name that tried into a refusal rather than a request quietly served from the pinned address

cases.input: an HTTPS origin answering 302 Location: http://10.0.0.1/internal
cases.note: 🛑 exit criterion 5 of 5. Refused on the 3xx itself, before the target is examined: re-validating after following is the shape of every SSRF bypass, where the second request is made by a layer that has forgotten the first one's constraints
IPv4-mapped IPv6. The same metadata address, spelled so that a deny list written in dotted quads does not recognise it

cases.input: https://[64:ff9b::a00:1]/repo.git
cases.note: NAT64 well-known prefix embedding 10.0.0.1; reaches RFC1918 through any NAT64 gateway

cases.input: https://x-access-token:ghp_0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz@github.com/acme/docs.git
cases.note: A token in the URL authority. Refused, not stripped: §8.5.7 supplies credentials through a file descriptor precisely so they never appear in a remote URL, and silently tidying it would hide from the operator that the token is already in their shell history

cases.input: a repository requesting recursive submodule cloning
cases.note: CVE-2025-48384 and CVE-2023-22490 are both reached by recursing into a submodule the operator never named. Recursion is not a setting with a safe default; GitSafety::submoduleArguments refuses the request loudly rather than silently doing the safe thing and leaving the caller believing recursion happened

cases.input: a build.os value of `ubuntu --privileged -v /:/host`
cases.note: 🛑 §8.5.14: the image is an allowlist KEY, never a reference, so a YAML value naming an image plus two flags never reaches argv at all - it reaches an array_key_exists. The first thing anyone tries against a build system that takes `build.os` from a repository

cases.input: a build command argument of `--privileged`
cases.note: Accepted as an ARGUMENT and refused as a FLAG. The image is the last flag-position element in the fixed argv template, so everything after it is the container's own argv and docker does not interpret it. Asserted by position rather than by rejection, because a legitimate command may contain a leading dash

cases.input:
a command argument containing a newline, e.g. `build
--privileged`
cases.expect: a command argument contains a control character
cases.note: A newline is how one argument becomes two lines in anything that logs or re-parses argv. Also refuses a NUL, which truncates at the execve boundary - everything after it is invisible to a check performed in PHP and still reaches the kernel

cases.input: a run specification for the `build` stage with accepts_stdin true
cases.expect: only the fetch stage may read a credential from stdin (§8.5.7)
cases.note: 🛑 The credential separation, as an invariant rather than a convention. Read the Docs runs post_checkout in the credentialed context; §8.5.7 says plainly that doing so voids the entire separation

cases.input: a post_checkout-shaped fixture in the build sandbox reading env, /run/cred, .git/config and grepping the workspace
cases.note: 🛑 Phase 06's exit criterion. The fetcher is given a sentinel credential on stdin; the build container then looks everywhere it could have survived - its own environment, the fetcher's tmpfs, the clone's .git/config - and finds none of it. CredentialIsolationTest, run in the runner container because the application image has no docker client

cases.input: a build container emitting a 20 MB log, and a single line of 64 KB
cases.note: §8.5.21: strip NUL bytes, truncate lines over 8 KiB, cap the log at 10 MiB. Enforced WHILE READING in the runner, not after: a cap applied once the bytes have crossed the spool is a cap on where they are stored rather than on what they cost
no signature at all
signature required on Response AND Assertion
XSW: a signed decoy alongside an unsigned injected assertion
exactly one Assertion is permitted
the assertion-id replay cache
XML comment in NameID splits the parsed value (CVE-2017-11427 class)
must never reach an entity-expanding parser
encrypted assertion without a signature
IdP-initiated is off by default
skew tolerance is 120s

cases.input: a build that forks without bound (`bomb() { bomb & bomb & }; bomb`)
cases.note: 🛑 The kernel refuses the forks at --pids-limit and the shell still EXITS 0, so `docker inspect` reports a clean run. `pids.events:max` in the cgroup is the only evidence it happened, and it has no daemon equivalent - which is why §8.5.15's 'read authoritatively from cgroup' is not a stylistic preference.

cases.input: a build writing 10 GB into its workspace
cases.note: 🛑 There is no portable filesystem quota to hand the kernel: --storage-opt needs overlay-on-xfs with pquota, and a tmpfs volume is remounted empty between stages (both measured, ADR 0011). So the runner measures the tree it can see and kills the container, which is enforcement rather than §8.5.18's 'unenforced soft limits'.

cases.input: a dependency install reaching deb.debian.org, which is not on the egress allowlist
cases.note: The allowlist carries package INDEXES (PyPI, npm, crates.io, the Go proxy, RubyGems) and git hosts. A distribution package manager is deliberately absent: §8.5.14 pre-bakes images, so a build installing system packages is a build doing something the image was supposed to have done.

cases.input: a build opening an outbound request to a host nobody allowlisted
cases.note: Refused by the CONNECT proxy with a 403, attributed to this build by the warden's address in the proxy's own access log - so the message can name the host rather than saying 'something was blocked'.

cases.input: a conf.py fetching http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ at import time
cases.note: 🛑 Its OWN identifier, distinct from any other blocked host, because the two need different words: an unreachable package index is a packaging problem and a build reaching for cloud instance credentials is an incident. Blocked twice over - the proxy refuses it and the nftables backstop drops the packet if the build goes round the proxy.

cases.input: a build that ignores http_proxy and opens a socket directly
cases.note: 🛑 Read from a named nft counter, not from the build's own words: 'Connection timed out' is what a dropped packet and a dependency server being down both look like. The counter distinguishes them, which is what makes the identifier stable enough to alert on.

cases.input: a spool document carrying `mounts: [/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock]`
cases.note: 🛑 Until Phase 07 an unrecognised spool field was IGNORED, which is safe only while the argv template stays exactly as narrow as it is today. Refusing means a document the constructor does not understand never runs - and the privilege-seeking names get their own identifier so an operator sees an attempt rather than a typo.

cases.input: a build that sleeps for twenty minutes
cases.note: Not retried (§8.5.16): a build that exceeded its clock once will exceed it again, and a retry buys a second slot for the same answer.

cases.input: a build container reaching ANOTHER build container on the sandbox network
cases.note: 🛑 The case an `internal: true` network does NOT close: internal means no route off the host, not no route across it. Two organisations' builds share that network, so without the per-build warden one could open a socket to the other's. Measured in ADR 0011.

cases.input: a sandbox from which the database is reachable
cases.note: §8.5.12 says 'Startup MUST fail', and a non-zero exit from the runner is how that reaches an init system. Demonstrated by attaching the database to the sandbox network and watching the self-test refuse.

cases.input: a token printed by a build, with a read boundary falling inside it
cases.note: 🛑 The reader buffers to the newline before anything sees a line, so a secret cannot straddle two records. Asserted by printing it two hundred times across half a megabyte - one split would show up as a missing occurrence and a usable fragment.

cases.input: a deploy key echoed as base64 by a failing fetch
cases.note: Base64 is how a key or a .netrc reaches a log and it has no shape a pattern could recognise - which is why SPEC 8.5.21 names the ENCODINGS and why SecretRegistry pre-computes them for values rather than matching on form.

cases.input: a build printing a NUL byte and a 64 KiB line
cases.expect: the NUL stripped, the line truncated at 8 KiB with a marker
cases.note: 🛑 A consequence worth knowing: a secret beyond 8 KiB of ONE line is discarded entirely rather than redacted, because truncation happens first. Safer, and the first version of the boundary test was wrong because it assumed otherwise.

cases.input: an anonymous reader requesting the build log of a members-only project with anonymous_build_logs=true
cases.note: 🛑 The setting WIDENS access to a project people can already read; it does not grant access to one they cannot. Both conditions, in that order.

cases.input: a revoked bearer token on the optionally-authenticated log endpoint
cases.note: 🛑 `optional` means no credential is acceptable, never that a wrong one is ignored. Falling through would silently downgrade a caller who believes they are authenticated - and the public view of a project is not the view they asked for.

cases.input: a build emitting more than 10 MiB of output
cases.note: 🛑 The middle is the right half to lose: the first lines say what the build was asked to do and the last say what went wrong. A naive stop-at-10-MiB - which Phase 06 shipped - loses the error on exactly the builds that need reading.

cases.input: a client whose cursor sits inside the gap the cap left
cases.note: The surviving sequence numbers are perfectly consistent on either side of the hole, so a client that is not told cannot tell. Measured against the first line actually RETURNED, not the first line in the file.

cases.input: fifty consecutive infrastructure failures of a project's default version
cases.expect: nothing disabled, and the counter unchanged
cases.note: 🛑 They neither increment NOR reset. Resetting is the intuitive implementation and it is wrong: our own outage would launder somebody's twenty-five consecutive broken configurations back to zero.

cases.input: a reader policy rule whose requirement is {"leaf": "gate", "driver": "ip_allowlist"}
cases.note: 🛑 The gate substituted for an identity. An IP allowlist is a network fact, never a principal, so a rule it alone satisfies authenticates nobody while reading as though it does.

cases.input: a requirement of {"any": [{"leaf": "gate"}, {"leaf": "binding"}]}
cases.note: 🛑 The shape that reads as safe and is not: 'from the office OR signed in' is 'from the office'. This is the one an operator writes on purpose, believing it adds a condition.

cases.input: a requirement of {"all": []}
cases.note: 🛑 The vacuous-truth fail-open §8.12.7 names by hand. An empty conjunction is TRUE in logic and reads as the strictest rule anybody could write, so it is refused at write time AND evaluates false at read time.

cases.input: a leaf declaring {"leaf": "binding", "driver": "ip_allowlist"}
cases.note: 🛑 §8.12.17 classifies each driver exactly once. A leaf contradicting the table would make the gate identity-bearing by a typo in a JSON payload rather than by any change to code.

cases.input: a domain_mounts.mount_exposure of 'public' on a project whose visibility is 'members'
cases.note: 🛑 Composition MUST NEVER widen access. Mounting a project on a second domain is otherwise a way to publish what the project's own visibility forbids.

cases.input: an anonymous request for a private resource on a project configured deny_status=403
cases.note: 🛑 403 is for authenticated principals only. A 403 to an anonymous request confirms the resource exists, which is what §8.2.7's absence-indistinguishable-from-non-existence refuses, and the project's own preference does not override it because the project does not bear the consequence.

cases.input: a handoff code redeemed a second time, with the same verifier
cases.note: 🛑 The code travels in a URL, so it reaches browser history, the Referer of anything the landing page loads, and every proxy log on the way. Single-use is what makes that leak worthless, and single-use has to be one atomic conditional write — a SELECT then an UPDATE has a race whose outcome is whether one code mints two sessions.

cases.input: a handoff code redeemed with a correctly-shaped verifier from another browser
cases.note: 🛑 RFC 7636's whole purpose, applied to DocUp's own handoff: the verifier exists only in a __Host-, HttpOnly cookie on the origin that started the exchange, so a leaked code is redeemable only by the browser that asked for it. 🛑 And the code is NOT consumed by a wrong verifier, or a probe would become a denial of service against the reader it was stolen from.

cases.input: a handoff with return=//evil.example/ (scheme-relative, so it does begin with a slash)
cases.note: 🛑 §8.12.10: the return URL is built from the verified domain row, never from a request parameter. This is the vector that gets missed — a browser reads //host/ as another origin and it passes a naive leading-slash check. The dashboard's handoff endpoint is the one place in the product that sends a reader across registrable domains, so an open redirect here carries the dashboard's authority.

cases.input: a grant minted for domain A, presented on domain B of the same project
cases.note: 🛑 The audience is the DOMAIN, not the project. Binding to the project reads just as naturally and would let one grant work on every domain a project serves — which is precisely the cross-origin reuse §8.12.10's per-origin handoff exists to prevent.

cases.input: a session handle set by a sibling subdomain and presented on another origin
cases.note: 🛑 §8.1.4's threat made concrete: documentation is attacker-controlled JavaScript, and on a shared parent domain it can toss a cookie at a sibling. __Host- is what stops the browser, and the server's own half is that `docs_sessions` is keyed on (project, domain) — so a tossed handle names a session that does not match even if the browser misbehaves.

cases.input: a signed, unexpired grant whose ep claim is below the project's current combined epoch
cases.note: 🛑 The signature is as valid as it was a moment ago; what changed is one integer in one row. This is how a policy edit or a session revoke takes effect on the next request with no purge — and the claim is the SUM of authz_epoch and identity_epoch, so either one moving is enough.

cases.input: a grant presented with alg: none and an empty signature
cases.note: 🛑 Refused structurally rather than by a check: the algorithm is a literal at both ends, so the token's own header never selects a verifier. §8.12.18 requires an algorithm allowlist excluding none; DocUp's own grant is the one token where that allowlist can be a singleton.

cases.input: a grant minted for the search surface, presented on the proxy surface
cases.note: 🛑 §8.12.21 disables a project's search entirely while its search generation lags its policy generation. A grant minted while reading a page must not route around that, so the surface is a claim and a mismatch is a refusal.

cases.input: a request to a project with a degraded password binding AND a healthy ip_allowlist binding that would admit it
cases.note: 🛑 "Never fall back to another provider, never to public." This is the case a naive merge gets wrong: the healthy allowlist admits the office network, so a project whose portal is broken keeps serving - a privacy posture nobody chose, from code that looks like graceful degradation. The degraded check therefore runs as its own pass over EVERY binding in scope before anything is merged, so it cannot be short-circuited by a binding that satisfied first.

cases.input: a binding transitioned to active with a passing probe and no human test login
cases.note: 🛑 "MUST NOT leave verifying until an automated probe passes AND a human completes a test login." The probe is the half a cron entry can do, so a path that accepted it alone would make the human half decorative - and the human half is the one that catches a provider answering correctly for the wrong directory.

cases.input: a probe that passes on a degraded binding, promoting it straight back to active
cases.note: 🛑 A recovered provider must not re-enter service unattended. The probe may move degraded to verifying and MUST NOT move anything to active: a provider that failed five times and then answered once has not been diagnosed, and an operator who was never told cannot have fixed it.

cases.input: a reader_credentials row inserted directly with kind=shared_link and expires_at NULL
cases.note: 🛑 Mandatory expiry, defended twice because the two defences fail differently: the application refusal can explain itself and the database CHECK survives a future writer who forgets the application. A share link is a bearer secret in a URL; without expiry it is a permanent grant to whoever the first recipient forwards it to.

cases.input: an expired share cookie presented for a private version of a public project
cases.note: 🛑 404, NOT 401. 8.12.23 permits a challenge for "an expired, revoked or out-of-scope share cookie" - permits, not requires - and 17 declines the permission here. The reason is what a share secret is: a credential that travels by being forwarded. A dead link answered with WWW-Authenticate tells whoever now holds it that the resource is real and guarded, and an expired link is the operator revocation taking effect, so that holder is an outsider by the operator own decision. An earlier revision of SharedLinkDriver returned a challengeable rejection here; the exit criterion own test is what found it.

cases.input: a live share link whose password is absent or wrong
cases.note: 🛑 The counterpart to provider-005, and the line between them is proof of the link. Once the secret has resolved the reader has demonstrated they hold a live link, so the existence of the resource is already certain to them and 8.12.16 passworded flow cannot offer a credential page without the challenge. Below that line - an unresolved secret - there is nothing to challenge for.

cases.input: two concurrent requests presenting the same max_uses=1 share link
cases.note: 🛑 Single-use must be one atomic conditional write. A SELECT then an UPDATE has a race whose outcome is whether a one-use link admits two readers, and for a single-use link that is the whole of its value. The guard therefore lives in the UPDATE own WHERE clause.

cases.input: a wrong password submitted repeatedly against the same credential from one address
cases.note: 🛑 Two properties in one case. The limiter is checked BEFORE the comparison, so a flood costs no Argon2 work - otherwise the rate limiter protects the credential and the CPU is the resource that falls over. And for a passworded link the password is verified only AFTER the secret resolves, so a wrong password against a link that does not exist costs one indexed prefix lookup: checking the password first would make the endpoint an Argon2 oracle for anybody sending noise.

cases.input: a reader policy rule written as {"leaf": "binding", "binding_id": X} where X is an ip_allowlist binding
cases.note: 🛑 8.12.17 classifies each driver exactly once and ip_allowlist is a gate, never an identity. Two defences meet here: the leaf is refused at write time against the classification table, and at read time a satisfied gate records no binding id at all - so a rule naming a gate binding cannot be satisfied by being on a network even if the write-time check were bypassed.

cases.input: an active binding whose envelope-encrypted secret cannot be opened (wrong kek_fingerprint)
cases.note: 🛑 Fail closed, and fail LOUD. An unreadable secret is indistinguishable from a provider outage from the reader side, so the binding becomes degraded rather than throwing a 500 or - far worse - being skipped as though it were not configured. A skipped binding is a guard that silently stopped guarding, which is the failure mode 8.12.19 exists to make impossible.

cases.input: a project-scoped password binding and an installation-scoped oidc binding, on the same project
cases.note: 🛑 Resolution is most-specific OF TYPE, not most-specific overall. Resolving one winner across all types would let a project add a password binding and thereby disable the installation identity provider for its own documentation - a privilege escalation performed by configuring something unrelated.

cases.input: a reader token presented as "Authorization: Token <T>", the Read the Docs form
cases.note: 20 lists this as a deliberate incompatibility: DocUp reads RFC 6750 Bearer only. 🛑 It is a corpus case rather than a compatibility note because the lenient parse is the tempting fix - and a parser that accepts several shapes is a parser whose shape an attacker chooses. Anything that is not exactly one Bearer token is nothing at all, not an error.

cases.input: an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ::ffff:127.0.0.1 presented against an ip_allowlist range of 127.0.0.0/8
cases.note: 🛑 The encoding a deny list written in dotted quads does not recognise, here in its mirror image: an allowlist comparison that normalised the mapped form would admit from a family the operator never entered. The comparison is on packed bytes with an explicit family check, so a v6 address never matches a v4 range in either direction. Compare git_url-016, the same encoding against the egress deny list.

cases.input: an id_token with alg:none, in both serialisations - three segments with an empty signature and two segments with none
cases.note: 🛑 The allowlist is a const with no code path that extends it, and the check runs on the token header BEFORE any key is fetched - so this costs no outbound request. Both serialisations are tried by real attackers and the two-segment form is the one a naive segment count misses. No library will emit either, which is why the corpus has to assemble them by hand: a test that produced them by passing odd arguments to an encoder would be testing the encoder.

cases.input: an id_token with alg:HS256, signed with the provider published RSA public key as the HMAC secret
cases.note: 🛑 The algorithm-confusion family, and the reason no HS* is in the allowlist. A published JWKS is public by definition, so a verifier that accepted a symmetric algorithm would let anybody who can read it mint an id_token. The same argument 8.12.11 makes for DocUp own grant - "an edge-held HMAC key makes every edge node a minter" - with more force, because the key is served to the world. Symmetric keys are also dropped from a key set before it is parsed, so there is no Key object for a confused verifier to reach.

cases.input: an id_token whose iss is the configured issuer with .attacker.test appended
cases.note: 🛑 Exact, by hash_equals, and the suffix form is the one a str_contains or str_ends_with check admits - RFC 9700 4.4 names it. The comparison is transitive through two steps: the discovery document own issuer is checked against the operator configured value (Discovery 4.3), and the token is checked against the document. A trailing slash is also a different string, because exact means exact.

cases.input: an id_token naming several audiences including this client, with no azp
cases.note: 🛑 The case that is a VALID token for somebody else. OIDC Core 3.1.3.7 step 4 requires azp when there is more than one audience, and without the check a token minted for another client at the same provider is replayable here - correctly signed, unexpired, and not for DocUp. A single audience needs no azp, so the check is conditional in exactly the way the specification makes it.

cases.input: an id_token with no at_hash, from a code-flow exchange
cases.note: 🛑 8.12.18 lists at_hash unconditionally where OIDC Core 3.3.2.11 requires it only for the hybrid flow, and the stricter reading is the right one: at_hash binds the id_token to the access token that arrived beside it, so a token PAIR cannot be assembled from two exchanges. Without it the access token DocUp holds is unbound from the identity DocUp believes it belongs to - and DocUp would call userinfo with it.

cases.input: an id_token whose kid names a key the provider does not publish, presented repeatedly
cases.note: 🛑 Two properties. The key is pinned, so a token cannot choose to be verified by a key it supplies and a provider holding ten keys does not get ten signature attempts. And the refresh is FLOORED: without a bound, an unknown kid is a free outbound request, so anybody who can reach a documentation host mints tokens with random kids and costs one HTTPS request each - a denial of service against the provider rate limit and against 8.3.9 egress budget. Five attempts cost two fetches, not five, and the next hundred inside the window cost none.

cases.input: an id_token with no kid at all
cases.note: 🛑 Reported as unpinnable rather than malformed, and the distinction is the requirement: "JWKS pinned by kid" cannot be satisfied by a token that names no key. Trying every published key instead - which some libraries do - gives an attacker as many signature attempts as the provider has keys.

cases.input: the same state presented twice to the callback, concurrently
cases.note: 🛑 Single-use as one atomic conditional write: the guard is in the UPDATE own WHERE, so two concurrent callbacks cannot both proceed. A SELECT then an UPDATE has the race whose outcome is whether one authorisation code mints two sessions. The second caller cannot tell "already consumed" from "expired" from "out of attempts", which is correct - all three mean the state is spent.

cases.input: a callback carrying id_token or access_token in the query
cases.note: 🛑 "No implicit flow", and the refusal happens BEFORE the state is consumed. That ordering is the interesting part: a forged redirect carrying a token must not be able to spend a real reader in-flight exchange, which would turn a refusal into a denial of service against the reader it was aimed at.

cases.input: a reader second request, served from a grant, against a rule naming a specific binding
cases.note: 🛑 Phase 24 found this FAILING. GrantVerifier parsed the bnd claim as raw 16 bytes while 8.12.6 requirement JSON holds UUID text and ReaderContext::satisfies compares strictly - so every binding-named rule was unsatisfiable on the grant path, which is every request after the first. The case is here as a 200 rather than a refusal because the defect was a denial: the corpus is for inputs that must be handled correctly, and "the same reader, the same URL, a different answer on the second request" is one.

cases.input: a project-scoped binding with a group mapping targeting the installation_owner role
cases.note: 🛑 8.12.5 own sentence is the threat model: "A project admin controls their own IdP; find-or-create-by-email would let any tenant mint an installation owner." A project admin configures a binding against a directory THEY control, so a project-scoped role mapping is not an escalation bug but an escalation feature - they would only have to add themselves to a group. Refused four times: the driver capability flag, the write-time validation invariant, a database CHECK, and again at login for a row predating all three.

cases.input: a reader who logs in a second time after being removed from a mapped group at the identity provider
cases.note: 🛑 "Reconciled - added AND removed - on every login", with the emphasis in the specification. The asymmetric implementation is what somebody writes without meaning to, and its failure mode is that leaving does not revoke: offboarding at the identity provider is the only offboarding most organisations perform. Only source=idp_mapping rows are touched, or a reconciliation would delete an operator manual grants.

cases.input: an id_token with no sub and a well-formed email claim
cases.note: 🛑 "email MUST NEVER be used for linking or lookup." The refusal matters because email is the obvious fallback and it is the one 8.12.1 names: a reader identity keyed on an email address would let a tenant whose directory they control assert any address they like. The subject is also stored as a keyed digest, so the readable value exists nowhere in DocUp - and the display label refuses anything containing an @ for the same reason.

cases.input: a binding whose issuer resolves to 169.254.169.254, or to a private address, or rebinds between resolution and connection
cases.note: 🛑 8.3.9 architecture test names this case by hand - "a second outbound path gets written in a hurry, for a webhook or an avatar fetch or an OIDC discovery document". An issuer URL is operator-supplied configuration naming a host DocUp will POST a client secret to, so it is exactly the input that one client exists for: resolve-then-pin, no redirects, a scheme allowlist and a byte cap. The egress rejection is translated rather than re-raised, because a reader login is not the place to report an operator misconfigured issuer in those terms.

cases.input: a provider authorization_endpoint carrying its own response_type=token query parameter
cases.note: 🛑 RFC 6749 3.1 permits a query on the authorization endpoint and some providers use one, so it is merged rather than clobbered - but DocUp parameters are merged OVER the provider, so an endpoint query cannot select the implicit flow or shadow redirect_uri. The harmless case (kc_idp_hint) survives; the dangerous one does not.
